concepts.title: List, Set, and Map: Choosing the Right Collection
concepts.description: List, Set, and Map are the three foundational collection interfaces in java.util, each with a distinct contract -- ordered and index-accessible, unordered and duplicate-free, or key-to-value lookup -- and picking ArrayList vs LinkedList, or a plain HashSet vs a sorted alternative, is really a decision about which operations need to be fast, not a stylistic preference.
learningObjectives: Explain the core contract each of List, Set, and Map guarantees, and choose the right one for a given data shape.
Explain the practical performance difference between ArrayList and LinkedList for common operations (indexed access, adding/removing at the end vs. in the middle).
Explain what makes an object usable as a HashSet element or HashMap key, in terms of equals() and hashCode() being consistent with each other.
Predict and explain a bug caused by using a mutable object as a HashMap key or HashSet element and then mutating it after insertion.
Use the core methods of List, Set, and Map (add/remove/get/contains, put/get/containsKey, iteration) correctly.
Explain why List and Set are declared as interface types on the left of a declaration (List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();) rather than the concrete implementation type.

sections.heading: Three Contracts, Three Shapes of Data
List Implementations: ArrayList vs LinkedList
sections.body:
`ArrayList` stores its elements in a resizable internal array -- indexed access (`list.get(i)`) is effectively instant regardless of the list's size, because it's just an array lookup at a computed offset. Adding an element at the *end* is normally instant too, except on the rare occasions the internal array is full and needs to be reallocated to a larger one (an occasional, amortized cost, not something you need to think about on every call). The cost shows up for insertion or removal in the *middle* or at the *front*: every element after that point has to be physically shifted over by one slot to make room (or to close the gap), which takes time proportional to how many elements come after the insertion point.

`LinkedList` stores elements as a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a link to the next (and previous) node. Adding or removing at the very front or back is instant, regardless of size, because it only ever touches the first or last node's links -- no shifting of anything else is required. But indexed access (`list.get(i)`) has to walk the chain from one end, node by node, until it reaches position `i` -- for a large list, `get(i)` on a `LinkedList` can be meaningfully slower than the equivalent `ArrayList` call, especially inside a loop that calls `get(i)` for every `i` (which effectively turns an intended linear scan into a much slower quadratic one).

The practical rule of thumb: default to `ArrayList` unless you specifically need frequent insertion/removal at the front, or you're implementing something like a queue or deque where a node-based structure is a genuinely better fit. Most everyday code that just accumulates elements and reads them back never actually needs LinkedList's specific strengths, which is why ArrayList is by far the more commonly reached-for default in real code.

sections.heading: Set and Map: equals() and hashCode() Have to Agree
The Mutable-Key Trap: Don't Change What You've Already Hashed

examples.title: List Permits Duplicates, Set Silently Rejects Them
examples.explanation: visits, a List, faithfully records every add() call in order, including the second "home" -- a List's contract has nothing to say about uniqueness, so all three entries exist, and size() correctly reports 3. Passing visits into new HashSet<>(visits) constructs a Set from that list's elements, and a Set's core contract -- no duplicates -- collapses the two "home" entries into one during construction; the resulting uniquePages has size 2, not 3. This is a common, genuinely useful pattern for deduplicating a list's contents: wrap it in a HashSet (or, if the original order matters, a LinkedHashSet) when you specifically need 'how many distinct values are there,' rather than writing manual duplicate-checking logic yourself.

examples.title: HashMap Requires equals()/hashCode() to Actually Find a Key
examples.explanation: The Product passed to get(...) is a brand-new object, constructed separately from the one originally put into the map -- it is not the same object in memory. Yet inventory.get(...) correctly finds and returns 5, because HashMap's lookup relies on hashCode() to locate the right bucket and equals() to confirm the match once there, and Product overrides both consistently based on sku. Had Product relied on Object's default, identity-based equals() and hashCode() (by simply not overriding them), this lookup would return null -- the two Product objects, despite representing the same SKU, would be considered entirely unrelated, since their default hash codes and default equals() checks are based on their distinct memory identities, not their content.

examples.title: The Mutable-Key Bug in Action
examples.explanation: The moment key.add("b") runs, the List's hashCode() (which List defines based on its current contents) changes -- but the HashMap's internal bucket structure was built using the hash code key had at the time it was inserted, and it has no way of knowing the key's hash code has since changed out from under it. The map still physically holds the entry, but containsKey(key) computes key's current (new) hash code, looks in the bucket that new hash code points to, and finds nothing there, because the entry is actually still sitting in the bucket the OLD hash code pointed to. This is exactly why mutable types like ArrayList make risky HashMap keys: the bug doesn't show up as an exception or an obvious error, just a silent, confusing 'the entry I definitely put in there seems to have vanished.'

misconceptions.description: A Set automatically keeps its elements sorted or in insertion order, since it's meant to represent a clean, well-organized collection of unique items.
misconceptions.clarification: Uniqueness and ordering are two completely separate guarantees, and plain Set (and its most common implementation, HashSet) only promises the first one. HashSet's iteration order is unspecified and driven by internal hash bucket placement -- it can appear essentially arbitrary and can even change between runs of the same program. If insertion order needs to be preserved, LinkedHashSet is the implementation that provides that guarantee; if elements need to come out in sorted order, TreeSet is the one to reach for. Assuming HashSet -- specifically -- maintains any particular order is a common, avoidable source of confusion when output 'looks wrong' despite every element genuinely being present.

misconceptions.description: Overriding equals() on a class is sufficient on its own to make that class work correctly as a HashSet element or HashMap key.
misconceptions.clarification: equals() and hashCode() have to be overridden together, consistently, or hash-based collections break in a specific, subtle way. The rule is: objects that are .equals() to each other MUST return the same hashCode(). If only equals() is overridden and hashCode() is left as the default (identity-based), two objects can be genuinely .equals() to each other yet still compute different hash codes -- which means a HashSet/HashMap can end up looking in the wrong bucket entirely when checking for a match, and contains()/get() can return false/null even for an object that, by .equals(), is clearly already present. Overriding one without the other doesn't just miss an optimization; it actively violates a contract the hash-based collections depend on to function correctly at all.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: numbers is a List -- does its contract remove or reject the duplicate 20 in any way when it's constructed?
unique is built by passing numbers into a HashSet constructor -- what does a Set's core contract do to duplicate values during that construction?

Trace the loop building countByValue step by step for each of the four numbers -- getOrDefault(n, 0) + 1 is incrementing a running count per distinct value, specifically tracking how many times 20 shows up.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 4, then 3, then 2. numbers keeps all four elements including the duplicate 20 (Lists allow duplicates). unique collapses the two 20s into one, giving 3 distinct values. countByValue counts occurrences per value, and 20 appears twice in numbers, so its count is 2.
exercises.solutionExplanation: numbers.size() is 4 because a List's contract never removes or rejects duplicates -- all four values passed to List.of(...) are present exactly as given. unique.size() is 3 because constructing a HashSet from numbers applies a Set's no-duplicates guarantee during construction, collapsing the two separate 20 entries down into a single element -- leaving 10, 20, and 30, three distinct values. countByValue.get(20) is 2 because the loop increments a running count for each value it encounters, using getOrDefault(n, 0) to start counting from 0 for a value seen for the first time; since 20 appears twice in numbers, its count is incremented twice, landing at 2.

exercises.prompt: This class is meant to let two Coordinate objects representing the same (x, y) position be treated as equal, and be usable correctly as keys in a HashMap. It compiles fine, but the assertion below fails. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Coordinate overrides equals() to compare x and y content -- but does it override hashCode() to match that same notion of equality?
Without a matching hashCode() override, Coordinate still inherits Object's default hashCode(), which is based on identity/memory address, not x and y.
Add a hashCode() override -- typically using Objects.hash(x, y) -- so that two Coordinates with the same x and y always produce the same hash code, matching what equals() already checks.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Coordinate overrides equals() to compare x and y by content, but never overrides hashCode(), so it still inherits Object's default, identity-based hashCode() -- meaning two Coordinate objects with identical x and y values, but different memory addresses, produce different hash codes. HashMap's containsKey() first computes the hash code of the Coordinate being looked up to find which bucket to search, and only then uses equals() to check candidates within that bucket -- if the new Coordinate(1, 1) hashes to a different bucket than the one actually holding the stored entry, equals() never even gets a chance to run, and containsKey() reports false despite the two objects clearly being .equals(). Adding a hashCode() override based on the same fields equals() uses (via Objects.hash(x, y)) guarantees that any two Coordinates that are .equals() also hash identically, letting HashMap actually find the right bucket and then confirm the match.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes when ArrayList is likely to be noticeably slower than LinkedList for the same sequence of operations?
options: Reading elements by index (get(i)) in a large loop -- ArrayList's array-based storage makes indexed access slow.

Inserting or removing an element near the FRONT of a large list repeatedly -- ArrayList has to shift every following element on each such operation, while LinkedList only updates a couple of node links.
Adding elements to the END of the list one at a time -- ArrayList cannot do this efficiently at all.
Iterating over every element in order with a for-each loop -- ArrayList is fundamentally incapable of sequential iteration.
assessments.explanation: Repeated insertion or removal near the front of an ArrayList forces every subsequent element to be physically shifted by one slot on each such operation, which costs time proportional to the list's size every single time -- LinkedList avoids this entirely for front operations, since it only ever has to relink a couple of node pointers, regardless of how many elements exist elsewhere in the list. Option A is backwards -- indexed get(i) is ArrayList's strength (a direct array-offset lookup) and LinkedList's weakness (it has to walk the chain). Option C is false -- appending to the end of an ArrayList is normally an instant, amortized-constant-time operation. Option D is false -- ArrayList iterates perfectly well in order; there's no fundamental incapacity there at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain why a class that overrides equals() to compare objects by their content, but doesn't also override hashCode(), can cause a HashSet or HashMap to behave incorrectly -- specifically, why a lookup can fail to find an object that is genuinely already present according to equals().
assessments.modelAnswer: HashSet and HashMap rely on hashing for fast operations: when an object is inserted, its hashCode() is computed and used to decide which internal storage bucket it goes into; when a lookup happens later, the hash code of the object being looked up is computed the same way, to figure out which single bucket needs to be searched, and only within that one bucket does equals() get used to check for an actual match against whatever else is already there. For this two-step process to work, there's a strict contract every class has to honor: any two objects that are .equals() to each other must produce the same hashCode(). If a class overrides equals() to compare by content but leaves hashCode() as Object's default -- which is based on the object's identity, essentially its memory address -- then two separately-constructed objects holding identical data will be .equals() to each other (since the content matches) but will very likely compute different hash codes (since they're different objects in memory). The practical consequence shows up at lookup time: inserting one such object stores it in whichever bucket its hash code points to; looking it up later via a different-but-equal object computes a different hash code and searches an entirely different bucket, where the original entry was never placed. Because the search never even reaches the bucket containing the real match, equals() never gets a chance to run and confirm anything -- the lookup reports 'not found' even though an equals()-equal object is sitting in the collection, just in the wrong bucket as far as this particular lookup's hash code is concerned. The fix is always to override hashCode() alongside equals(), deriving both from the exact same set of fields, so that equal objects are guaranteed to compute equal hash codes and therefore always land in, and get searched in, the same bucket.

assessments.prompt: Set<String> tags = new HashSet<>(); boolean firstAdd = tags.add("java"); boolean secondAdd = tags.add("java"); System.out.println(firstAdd + " " + secondAdd); What prints?
options: true true, because add() always returns true whenever it's given a valid, non-null argument.

true false, because add() returns whether the element was actually newly added -- the first call adds "java" and returns true, the second call finds it already present, does nothing, and returns false.
This throws an exception on the second add() call, because Set forbids adding a value that's already a duplicate.
false true, because add() reports whether the set's size changed as a result of the call, and duplicate detection happens only after size is already checked.
assessments.explanation: A Set's core contract guarantees no duplicates, and add() communicates whether it actually changed anything by returning a boolean: true if the element was genuinely new and got added, false if an equal element was already present and the call was silently a no-op. The first add("java") has nothing to collide with yet, so it succeeds and returns true; the second finds "java" already there, changes nothing, and returns false. Option A is wrong because add() specifically reports success or no-op, not a constant true. Option C is wrong because attempting to add a duplicate is not an error condition in Java -- it's an ordinary, silent no-op. Option D garbles the actual mechanism; there's no separate 'size check before duplicate check' step.

assessments.prompt: List<Integer> key = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1)); Map<List<Integer>, String> map = new HashMap<>(); map.put(key, "first"); key.add(2); System.out.println(map.get(key)); What is the most likely outcome, and why?
options: "first" -- HashMap always finds a key by checking every stored entry one by one with equals(), so mutating the key afterward doesn't matter.

Often null -- mutating key after insertion changes its hashCode() (since List's hash code depends on its current contents), so get(key) computes a different bucket than the one the entry was actually stored under at insertion time, and the lookup fails to find it.
This throws a ConcurrentModificationException, since a list that's currently a live map key can never be mutated.
"first" -- HashMap automatically detects the mutation and re-hashes every affected key entry on the spot.
assessments.explanation: HashMap locates entries by computing a key's hash code to pick a bucket, and List's hashCode() is defined in terms of its current elements -- so key.add(2) changes what key.hashCode() returns. The entry itself is still physically sitting in the bucket the original hash code pointed to, but map.get(key) computes key's new, current hash code and looks in a different bucket, one that was never given this entry. Nothing throws; the lookup simply fails silently. Option A misdescribes HashMap's actual lookup mechanism, which is bucket-based, not a scan of every entry. Option C invents a protection Java's mutable collections don't have. Option D describes a re-hashing-on-mutation feature that HashMap does not implement -- it has no way to even detect that a key it's holding was just mutated elsewhere.

assessments.prompt: Why is List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); generally preferred over ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); for a local variable only ever used through basic List operations?
options: There's no real difference at all; it's purely a stylistic preference with no practical consequence either way.

Declaring the variable's type as the interface means every use of names is checked only against List's contract, so the concrete implementation on the right-hand side can later be swapped (to LinkedList, say) by changing just that one line, without touching any other code that only ever called List methods on names.
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); actually fails to compile, since a variable's declared type is required to be an interface whenever a generic collection is involved.
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); runs measurably faster at run time, since interface-typed method calls skip virtual dispatch entirely.
assessments.explanation: Declaring the left-hand type as the interface deliberately restricts what the rest of the code is allowed to assume about names -- only List's own contract, nothing ArrayList-specific. That's precisely what makes swapping the concrete implementation later a one-line change: as long as every other use of names only ever called List methods, changing just the right-hand side to new LinkedList<>() keeps everything else compiling and working unchanged. Option A understates a real, practical software-engineering benefit. Option C is simply false -- declaring a variable with a concrete class type is completely legal Java. Option D is fabricated; there is no such blanket run-time performance difference from the declared type of a reference variable.

concepts.title: Generics and Type Erasure
concepts.description: Generics let a class or method be parameterized by a type, catching type mismatches at compile time instead of at a runtime ClassCastException -- but the compiler achieves this by erasing all that type information after compilation, and understanding exactly what type erasure removes (and what it doesn't) explains several otherwise-baffling generics restrictions and warnings.
learningObjectives: Explain what problem generics solve, contrasted with a pre-generics collection of Object with manual casting.
Declare and use a generic class and a generic method with a type parameter, and explain what a bounded type parameter (<T extends Comparable<T>>) adds.
Explain type erasure: what the compiler does with type parameter information after compile time, and why List<String> and List<Integer> share exactly one Class object at run time.
Predict and explain why you cannot create a generic array (new T[10]) directly, and why instanceof cannot check against a parameterized type.
Explain wildcard basics (? extends T vs ? super T) at a conceptual level -- reading from a producer vs writing to a consumer.
Predict the exact unchecked-cast or compile-time behavior of a small generics code snippet involving erasure.

sections.heading: The Problem Generics Solve: Casting Everywhere, Caught Too Late
sections.body:
Before generics (pre-Java 5), a general-purpose container like a `List` could only actually hold `Object` references -- there was no way to tell the compiler 'this specific list only ever holds `String`s.' Reading an element back out required an explicit cast, and that cast was purely a promise the programmer made to the compiler, with no compiler-enforced backing at all:

```java
List names = new ArrayList();      // pre-generics style -- holds raw Objects
names.add("Amy");
names.add(42);                       // compiles fine -- nothing stops a wrong type from going in

String first = (String) names.get(0);   // fine
String second = (String) names.get(1);  // compiles fine, throws ClassCastException at RUN TIME
```

The bug -- putting an `Integer` into a list that was only ever *meant* to hold `String`s -- is invisible at the point where it actually happens (`names.add(42);` compiles without complaint, since `names` is declared to hold any `Object`), and only surfaces much later, at the cast, potentially in a completely different part of the program, as a runtime `ClassCastException`. Generics close this gap by letting you tell the compiler the intended element type up front: `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` makes `names.add(42);` itself a compile-time error -- `42` (an `int`, autoboxed to `Integer`) simply isn't a `String`, and the mistake is caught at the exact line where it's actually made, not wherever the value happens to get read back out later.

sections.heading: Generic Classes and Methods: Parameterizing Over a Type
Type Erasure: Generics Are a Compile-Time Illusion
sections.body:
Here is the detail that explains almost every 'weird' generics restriction you'll run into: Java implements generics through **type erasure**. The compiler uses your type parameters (`<T>`, `<String>`, whatever) to check your code for type correctness *at compile time*, and then, when producing the actual bytecode, it **erases** that information -- a type parameter with no bound is simply replaced with `Object` everywhere it's used, and all the casts needed to make that safe are inserted automatically by the compiler. At run time, there is no `T` anywhere in the compiled `.class` file at all.

The single most concrete, checkable consequence: `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are backed by the exact same `.class` file (well, its implementation, like `ArrayList.class`), and produce the exact same `Class` object at run time:

```java
List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> integers = new ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(strings.getClass() == integers.getClass());   // true!
```

This is genuinely surprising the first time you see it -- it looks like these should be two different types, since the compiler treats them so differently -- but by the time the JVM is actually running the program, both variables' run-time class is just `ArrayList`, full stop; the `<String>` and `<Integer>` information existed purely for the compiler's own type-checking and was thrown away afterward. This is also, precisely, why `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` cannot be used as two separate overloads (`void process(List<String> l)` and `void process(List<Integer> l)` in the same class is a compile error, 'name clash') -- after erasure, both methods would have the exact same erased signature, `process(List)`, and Java cannot have two methods with identical signatures.

sections.heading: What Erasure Forbids: Generic Arrays and instanceof Against a Parameterized Type
Wildcards: ? extends T (Producer) and ? super T (Consumer)
sections.body:
Wildcards let a method accept a *range* of related parameterized types rather than one exact one. `List<? extends Number>` means 'a `List` of some unknown specific type that is `Number` or a subtype of it' -- you can safely *read* elements out of it (each one is guaranteed to be at least a `Number`), but you cannot safely *add* to it (the list's real element type might specifically be `Integer`, and adding a plain `Double` would violate that, so the compiler forbids adding anything at all, to stay safe). `List<? super Integer>` means 'a `List` of some unknown type that is `Integer` or a supertype of it' -- you can safely *add* `Integer`s to it (any such list is guaranteed to be able to hold an `Integer`), but reading from it only gives you back `Object` (the compiler can't promise anything more specific than that about what's actually stored).

The common mnemonic is **PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super** -- if your method is treating the parameterized collection as a source of values it reads (a 'producer'), use `? extends T`; if it's treating the collection as a destination it writes into (a 'consumer'), use `? super T`. A method like `double sum(List<? extends Number> numbers)` only ever reads from `numbers` to add up a total, so `? extends Number` is exactly right -- it lets callers pass a `List<Integer>`, a `List<Double>`, or a `List<Number>` itself, all of which the plain, unbounded `List<Number>` parameter type would have rejected.

examples.title: Erasure Means List<String> and List<Integer> Are the Same Class at Run Time
examples.explanation: getClass() reports the object's actual, run-time class -- and for both strings and integers, that's simply ArrayList, with no trace of String or Integer anywhere in it. The <String> and <Integer> that appear in the source code are compile-time-only information: javac uses them to check that only Strings are ever added to strings and only Integers to integers, and to avoid you having to write manual casts when reading elements back out -- but that checking is finished by the time compilation ends, and the resulting bytecode makes no distinction between the two lists at all. This is the literal, concrete meaning of type erasure: the type parameter is 'erased' from the compiled artifact, leaving behind only whatever raw type (here, effectively Object, since List<T> has no bound) the parameter stood in for.

examples.title: A Bounded Type Parameter Enables a Generic Max-Finder
examples.explanation: <T extends Comparable<T>> tells the compiler that whatever T ends up being, it must implement Comparable<T> -- which is exactly what makes item.compareTo(largest) legal inside the method body; without that bound, T could be any type at all, including ones with no compareTo() method whatsoever, and the method simply wouldn't compile. Integer and String both implement Comparable<Integer> and Comparable<String> respectively (as part of the standard library), so max() works correctly for both List<Integer> and List<String> -- one single method definition, type-checked once, reused for every type that satisfies the bound. Passing a List of some type that does NOT implement Comparable would fail at the call site itself, at compile time, with a clear type-bound violation -- not as a runtime surprise deep inside the loop.

examples.title: PECS in Practice: A Producer Parameter and a Consumer Parameter
examples.explanation: sum() only ever reads elements out of numbers (via the for-each loop) to accumulate a total, so it's a producer of values from the caller's point of view -- ? extends Number lets it accept a List<Integer>, a List<Double>, or a List<Number> itself, any of which is guaranteed to hand back something that's at least a Number when read. A plain List<Number> parameter would have rejected List<Integer> entirely, since List<Integer> is not actually a subtype of List<Number> in Java's type system, despite Integer being a subtype of Number. fillWithSquares() only ever writes into destination, so it's a consumer -- ? super Integer lets it accept a List<Number> or List<Object>, either of which is guaranteed to be able to hold an Integer safely, without needing destination to be exactly List<Integer>. Trying to read a specific type back out of a ? super Integer parameter would only ever give you Object, which is why consumer-style wildcards are for writing, not reading.

misconceptions.description: Because List<String> and List<Integer> are clearly different, incompatible types at compile time, they must also be different classes at run time, each with their own distinct Class object.
misconceptions.clarification: This is exactly backwards from how type erasure actually works. The compiler enforces the distinction between List<String> and List<Integer> entirely during compilation -- checking every add() and assignment against the declared type parameter -- and then discards that type parameter information when producing bytecode. At run time, both are represented by the exact same class (typically ArrayList, or whatever concrete implementation was used), and calling .getClass() on either returns the identical Class object. The type safety generics provide is a compile-time guarantee about how your source code is allowed to use a collection, not a run-time property the JVM can inspect or distinguish between afterward.

misconceptions.description: You should be able to write if (someList instanceof List<String>) to check, at run time, whether a list specifically holds Strings.
misconceptions.clarification: This specific check is a compile-time error in Java, not merely bad practice -- because of type erasure, there is no run-time representation of the parameterized type List<String> distinct from plain List for the JVM to check against; the <String> part simply doesn't exist anymore once compilation is finished. The compiler only permits the unparameterized check, someList instanceof List, which tells you it's a List of *something*, with no way to ask what that something specifically is via instanceof. If you genuinely need to verify element types at run time, that requires manually inspecting individual elements (e.g., checking each element with instanceof String) rather than trying to check the collection's declared type parameter, which was never preserved past compile time.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: Both namesPair and numbersPair are instances of the same generic class Pair -- but with different type arguments. After type erasure, is there any run-time difference between Pair<String> and Pair<Integer> as far as .getClass() is concerned?
getClass() reports the actual run-time class, which is unaffected by which type argument was used to construct a particular Pair instance.
namesPair.getFirst() returns a T that the compiler already knows, from namesPair's declared type, must be a String -- so no explicit cast is needed to call a String-specific method on it.
exercises.expectedAnswer: true, then AMY. namesPair and numbersPair are both run-time instances of the same erased class Pair, so their getClass() results are identical, regardless of the different type arguments used when constructing each one. namesPair.getFirst() returns "Amy", and .toUpperCase() on it gives "AMY".
exercises.solutionExplanation: Pair<String> and Pair<Integer> are both, after erasure, simply instances of the one class Pair -- the type argument used at construction time (String or Integer) has no bearing on the object's actual run-time class, so namesPair.getClass() == numbersPair.getClass() is true, exactly analogous to List<String> and List<Integer> sharing ArrayList.class. Separately, namesPair.getFirst() returns the value stored in first for that specific instance, "Amy" -- and because namesPair was declared as Pair<String>, the compiler already knows getFirst()'s return type is specifically String for this call, inserting whatever cast is needed automatically, so calling .toUpperCase() directly on the result compiles and runs without any explicit cast being written, producing "AMY".

exercises.prompt: This generic Stack class is meant to store items in a plain array internally, but it fails to compile. Find and fix the bug, explaining why the original line is illegal.
hints: Creating an array requires the JVM to know a real, concrete element type at run time -- does T still exist as a real type at run time, after type erasure?
The standard workaround for this exact situation is to back the generic class with an Object array internally instead of a T array.
You'll need an explicit, compiler-flagged-as-unchecked cast back to T when reading an element out of the Object array in pop().
exercises.solutionExplanation: new T[capacity] is illegal because, after type erasure, T no longer exists as a real type at the point the array would actually be created -- the JVM needs a genuine, concrete element type to allocate an array (arrays track their element type at run time for array-store checks), and there's nothing left for T to be at that point. The standard, idiomatic workaround, used internally by real generic collection classes like ArrayList, is to back the class with a plain Object[] instead, which is always a legal, concrete array type to create. push() stores items into that Object[] without needing any cast (every T is already an Object). pop(), however, needs to hand back a T to its caller, and reading an Object out of items and treating it as a T requires an explicit cast, (T) items[--size] -- one the compiler cannot fully verify is safe at run time (since T is erased), which is exactly why it's paired with @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") to acknowledge that the class's own internal logic (only ever storing T values via push()) is what actually guarantees the cast's safety, not anything the compiler itself can check.

assessments.prompt: Why does Java forbid writing if (someList instanceof List<String>)?
options: Because instanceof can never be used with any interface type, generic or not.
Because after type erasure, there is no run-time representation of List<String> distinct from plain List -- the JVM has nothing to check the parameterized type against.
Because List<String> is not actually a subtype of List at run time.
Because instanceof only works on final classes, and List is an interface.
assessments.explanation: Type erasure removes type parameter information from the compiled bytecode -- at run time, an ArrayList holding Strings and an ArrayList holding Integers are represented by the exact same class, with nothing distinguishing 'holds Strings specifically' as a run-time-checkable property. Since instanceof fundamentally asks a run-time question ('is this object an instance of this run-time type'), and List<String> as a distinct run-time type simply does not exist post-erasure, the compiler rejects the check outright rather than let it silently do something less than what it appears to ask. Option A is false -- instanceof works fine with interfaces generally (unparameterized ones, like plain List, are checked constantly). Option C is a nonsensical claim about subtyping, not the actual reason. Option D is fabricated -- instanceof has no such final-class restriction.

assessments.prompt: Explain type erasure to a developer who is confused about why they can't create a generic array (new T[10]) inside a generic class, even though the class compiles fine everywhere else it uses T.
assessments.modelAnswer: Java implements generics using type erasure: the compiler uses your type parameters, like T in a generic class, to check that your code uses types consistently while you're writing and compiling it, but once compilation finishes, that type parameter information is discarded from the resulting bytecode. Wherever an unbounded T appeared in your source, the compiled class effectively treats it as Object, inserting whatever casts are needed automatically so the erased code still behaves correctly. This is why, for instance, List<String> and List<Integer> end up being represented by the exact same run-time class -- there's no T, no String, no Integer baked into the compiled class file at all; that information only ever existed for the compiler's own benefit, during the one phase where it's actually checking your code. The reason this specifically breaks new T[10] is that creating an array in Java is not just about type-checking -- arrays are required to know their own real, concrete element type at run time, so that the JVM can perform array-store checks (rejecting, say, an attempt to put a String into an Integer[] at run time). By the time new T[10] would actually execute, T has already been erased and no longer corresponds to any real type the JVM could give the new array as its element type -- there's simply nothing concrete left to create an array of. This is precisely why generic classes that need an internal array, like the standard library's own ArrayList, are implemented by creating a plain Object[] internally instead, and inserting an explicit (marked-unchecked) cast back to T whenever an element needs to be handed back out to a caller as that specific type -- a workaround that only exists because of, and only makes sense once you understand, type erasure.

assessments.prompt: List names = new ArrayList(); names.add("Amy"); names.add(42); String first = (String) names.get(0); String second = (String) names.get(1); Which line is the actual root cause of the bug here, and when does the problem actually surface?
options: names.add(42); is the root cause, and the compiler catches it immediately at that exact line, before the program can even run.

names.add(42); is the root cause -- a value of the wrong intended type entering the raw, unparameterized list -- but with no type parameter for the compiler to check against, this line compiles without complaint; the problem only surfaces later, as a ClassCastException at the cast on a following line, in a different part of the code from where the actual mistake was made.
String second = (String) names.get(1); is the root cause, since casts are inherently unsafe and should never appear in correct code.
There is no actual bug here; this code compiles and runs correctly, printing normally.
assessments.explanation: names is declared as a raw List, with no element type parameter for the compiler to enforce -- so names.add(42) compiles just as readily as names.add("Amy") did, since both are legal Objects as far as an unparameterized List is concerned. The actual mistake -- putting an Integer into a list only ever meant to hold Strings -- is invisible right where it happens. It only becomes visible much later, when (String) names.get(1) tries to cast that Integer to String and the JVM throws ClassCastException at run time, in code that may be far removed from the add() call that actually caused the problem. Option A wrongly assumes the compiler tracks intended element types on a raw list. Option C blames the cast itself rather than the type mismatch the cast merely exposes. Option D is wrong because this exact sequence is precisely the runtime-ClassCastException bug generics were introduced to catch earlier.

assessments.prompt: public static <T> T max(List<T> items) { T largest = items.get(0); for (T item : items) { if (item.compareTo(largest) > 0) { largest = item; } } return largest; } Why does this specific method fail to compile as written?
options: It compiles fine exactly as written, for any type T supplied at the call site.

T has no bound here, so the compiler only knows T is some type extending Object -- and Object declares no compareTo() method, so item.compareTo(largest) doesn't resolve to any method the compiler can find; T needs to be declared as <T extends Comparable<T>> for that call to be legal.
for-each loops can never be used with a type parameter that has no explicit bound, under any circumstance.
List<T> is illegal syntax on a method parameter; it must be written as List<? extends T> instead.
assessments.explanation: With no bound on T, all the compiler can assume about it is that it's some subtype of Object -- and Object has no compareTo() method at all, so item.compareTo(largest) fails to compile, since there's no guarantee whatever type T ends up being actually supports that call. Adding a bound, <T extends Comparable<T>>, restricts T to only types that do implement Comparable<T>, which is exactly what makes compareTo() a legal call inside the method body. Option A ignores this missing bound entirely. Option C is fabricated -- for-each loops work fine over List<T> regardless of any bound on T; the failure is specifically about calling compareTo(), not about iterating. Option D is wrong -- List<T> as an ordinary parameter type is completely standard generic syntax.

assessments.prompt: A method needs to copy every element out of a source list into a destination list, only ever reading from source and only ever writing into destination, without requiring either list to be an exact type match for T. Following PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super), which parameter types are correct for static <T> void copy(source, destination)?
options: List<? super T> source, List<? extends T> destination -- source produces values, so it should use super, and destination consumes them, so it should use extends.

List<? extends T> source, List<? super T> destination -- source is only ever read from (a producer of values), so it uses extends; destination is only ever written into (a consumer of values), so it uses super.
List<T> source, List<T> destination -- wildcards are never appropriate when copying between two lists that share the same type parameter T.
List<? extends T> source, List<? extends T> destination -- both parameters should use extends, since both are Lists related to T.
assessments.explanation: PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. source is only read from inside copy(), producing the values being moved -- so ? extends T is correct, letting callers pass a List<Integer> or any other subtype-of-T list as the source. destination is only written into, consuming those values -- so ? super T is correct, letting callers pass a List<Number> or any other supertype-of-T list as the destination, as long as it's guaranteed able to hold a T. Option A reverses the two roles entirely. Option C would work but is needlessly restrictive, forcing both lists to be exactly List<T> when callers might reasonably want to pass related, non-identical types. Option D would let source work correctly but would break destination, since adding a T to a List<? extends T> is exactly the operation Java's wildcard rules forbid, for safety.

concepts.title: Comparable vs. Comparator
concepts.description: Comparable defines a class's own single, natural ordering via compareTo(), baked into the class itself, while Comparator defines an ordering from the outside -- letting the same objects be sorted in as many different ways as you need, without ever touching the class being sorted.
learningObjectives: Implement Comparable<T> on a class to define its natural ordering, and explain what compareTo()'s return value's sign (negative/zero/positive) actually means.
Write a Comparator<T> as a separate object to sort the same class in a different, non-natural order, using both a class and a lambda.
Use Comparator's chaining methods (thenComparing, reversed) to build a multi-key sort without writing a manual multi-condition compareTo.
Explain why a class can have only one natural ordering (one compareTo()) but arbitrarily many Comparators.
Predict the outcome of Collections.sort()/List.sort() given a specific Comparable implementation or Comparator, including sorting in descending order.
Identify and fix a broken compareTo() implementation that violates the required sign contract, such as through unsafe subtraction.

sections.heading: Comparable<T>: A Class's Own, Single Natural Ordering
Comparator<T>: Ordering Defined From the Outside, as Many Ways as You Need
sections.body:
A class can implement `Comparable` at most once -- it has exactly one natural order, full stop. But real programs routinely need to sort the *same* objects different ways in different contexts: employees by salary in one report, by name in another. `Comparator<T>` is a completely separate object -- not a method on the class being sorted at all -- that defines one specific ordering, and you can write as many `Comparator`s for a given type as you have sorting needs.

```java
Comparator<Employee> byNameLambda = (a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName());

employees.sort(byNameLambda);
System.out.println(employees);   // sorted by name, completely independent of Employee's own compareTo()
```

Crucially, `Employee` itself needs no changes at all to support this -- `byNameLambda` lives entirely outside the class, and `List.sort(Comparator<T>)` uses it in preference to whatever `compareTo()` the elements might also define. This is the core structural difference to internalize: `Comparable` is a capability the class author bakes in once, representing the *one* ordering the class considers 'natural'; `Comparator` is a capability any caller can define, on demand, from outside the class, and nothing stops several different, unrelated pieces of code from each defining their own `Comparator<Employee>` for their own specific purposes, with zero coordination or changes to `Employee` needed.

sections.heading: Chaining Comparators: thenComparing and reversed, Instead of a Manual Multi-Key compareTo
sections.body:
Sorting by more than one key -- 'by grade, then by GPA within each grade' -- used to mean writing a manual `compareTo`-style method with an if/else cascade checking each key in turn. `Comparator`'s default methods (`thenComparing`, `reversed`, and the static factory method `comparing`) build this compositionally, without any manual cascade at all:

```java
Comparator<Student> byGradeThenGpaDesc = Comparator
        .comparing((Student s) -> s.grade)
        .thenComparing(s -> s.gpa, Comparator.reverseOrder());

students.sort(byGradeThenGpaDesc);
```

`Comparator.comparing(s -> s.grade)` builds a `Comparator` that compares two `Student`s by whatever `grade` holds (relying on that field's own natural ordering -- `String`'s, here); `.thenComparing(s -> s.gpa, Comparator.reverseOrder())` chains a second key that's only consulted to break ties when the first comparison result is exactly zero (same grade), and orders that tie-break by descending GPA. `.reversed()` on any `Comparator` produces a new one with the ordering flipped entirely, without needing a separate, hand-written 'descending' version of the same comparison logic. This compositional style avoids an entire class of bugs that hand-written multi-condition `compareTo`/`compare` methods are prone to -- specifically, forgetting to handle the tie-break case correctly, or getting the sign backwards in one branch of a large if/else chain.

sections.heading: A Broken compareTo(): Contract Violations That Corrupt Sorting Silently

examples.title: Comparable Gives a Class Its Natural Order
examples.explanation: Collections.sort(tasks) needs no second argument specifying how to compare Tasks, because Task itself declares its natural order via compareTo(), which compares by priority ascending using Integer.compare -- a safe alternative to this.priority - other.priority that avoids any risk of overflow for extreme int values. The sort correctly orders tasks from lowest priority number (1, 'Fix bug') to highest (3, 'Deploy'), entirely because compareTo() returns a negative, zero, or positive result reflecting exactly that intended ordering for every pair of tasks Collections.sort happens to compare during the sort.

examples.title: The Same Objects, Sorted Two Different Ways With Two Comparators
examples.explanation: Neither sort() call here touches Task's own compareTo() at all -- both pass an explicit Comparator instead, which List.sort() uses in place of the elements' natural ordering entirely. Comparator.comparing(Task::getName) builds a Comparator directly from a method reference, comparing tasks by whatever getName() returns using String's own natural (alphabetical) order; the second sort uses Comparator.comparingInt(Task::getPriority).reversed() to sort by priority but flip the direction, so higher priority numbers come first instead of the ascending order Task's own compareTo() would produce. The same three Task objects get reordered completely differently by each call, with Task's source code never changing at all -- this is the entire point of keeping ordering logic external to the class via Comparator, rather than being limited to whatever single order compareTo() happens to define.

examples.title: Multi-Key Sorting With thenComparing
examples.explanation: The primary key is grade, sorted in its natural (alphabetical) ascending order via Comparator.comparing, which groups Amy and Cara (both grade A) ahead of Ben (grade B). Within that A group, thenComparing(s -> s.gpa, Comparator.reverseOrder()) only gets consulted as a tie-breaker for pairs whose grade comparison already returned zero -- Amy and Cara -- and it orders that specific subgroup by gpa in descending order, putting the higher GPA first: Cara (3.9) before Amy (3.8). Ben, having a different grade entirely, is never compared against them by gpa at all; the grade comparison alone already placed him last, after both A-grade students. The final order is therefore Cara, then Amy, then Ben.

misconceptions.description: A class can implement Comparable multiple times, or in multiple ways, to support different orderings for different situations.
misconceptions.clarification: A class can implement Comparable<T> exactly once -- it's a single method, compareTo(), and a class either has one natural ordering or none at all; there's no mechanism to define several different compareTo() overloads or variants for different contexts. When a class genuinely needs to be sorted in more than one way, the natural ordering (if any) belongs in compareTo(), and every other ordering is expressed as a separate Comparator object, defined wherever it's actually needed, entirely independent of the class itself and of each other.

misconceptions.description: Since sorting just needs SOME consistent order, the exact numeric value returned by compareTo() (not just its sign) matters and gets used by sorting algorithms.
misconceptions.clarification: Only the sign of compareTo()'s return value is ever meaningful -- negative, zero, or positive -- never its magnitude. Returning -1 versus -1000000 for 'this comes before other' produces identical sorting behavior; no sorting algorithm or sorted collection in the standard library ever inspects or uses the actual numeric size of the returned value for anything. This matters practically because it means overly-clever-looking compareTo() implementations that try to encode 'how much bigger' one object is than another via the return value's magnitude are not doing anything sorting-relevant with that extra information -- it's simply discarded by every consumer of compareTo().

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: Collections.sort(players) with no second argument uses whatever natural ordering Player defines via compareTo() -- what field does that compare by, and in which direction?
The second sort call passes an explicit Comparator built from p.name -- this completely overrides compareTo() for this one call; it does not combine with it.
String's natural (alphabetical) order is what Comparator.comparing((Player p) -> p.name) actually uses to compare the extracted name values.
exercises.expectedAnswer: [Kim:50, Lee:65, Jo:80] then [Jo:80, Kim:50, Lee:65]. The first sort uses compareTo(), ordering ascending by score. The second sort uses an explicit Comparator by name, completely replacing the score-based order with alphabetical order by name.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Collections.sort(players) with no explicit Comparator falls back to each element's own compareTo(), which Player defines to compare by score ascending -- so the first printed list orders Kim(50), Lee(65), Jo(80) from lowest to highest score. The second sort call passes Comparator.comparing((Player p) -> p.name) explicitly, which entirely replaces the ordering used for this call -- it does not defer to or combine with compareTo() in any way. That Comparator extracts each Player's name and compares using String's natural alphabetical order, giving Jo, Kim, Lee alphabetically, so the second printed list is [Jo:80, Kim:50, Lee:65], completely unrelated to the score-based order from the line before it.

exercises.prompt: This compareTo() implementation is meant to sort Products by price ascending, but sorting a large list of Products with extreme price values occasionally produces an incorrectly-ordered result. Find and fix the bug.
hints: this.priceInCents - other.priceInCents is ordinary int subtraction -- what happens if the true mathematical difference between two extreme int values doesn't actually fit in an int?
int overflow wraps around silently in Java -- no exception is thrown -- which can flip the sign of the result compared to what the true difference would have been.
Use the dedicated Integer.compare(a, b) static method instead, which is specifically designed to return the correct sign without any overflow risk.
exercises.solutionExplanation: this.priceInCents - other.priceInCents computes the mathematical difference using ordinary int arithmetic, which has a fixed range -- if priceInCents holds values near Integer.MAX_VALUE and Integer.MIN_VALUE respectively (or close enough to those extremes), the true difference can exceed what an int can represent, and Java's int arithmetic silently wraps around (overflows) rather than throwing any error. That wraparound can flip the sign of the result entirely, making compareTo() report 'this is smaller' when it's actually larger, or vice versa -- which corrupts the sort for exactly those extreme-value pairs while appearing to work correctly for every ordinary-sized value, making the bug easy to miss in casual testing. Integer.compare(a, b) is implemented specifically to avoid this: it returns the correct sign for any two int values without ever performing a subtraction that could overflow, which is exactly why it -- along with Double.compare, Long.compare, and the other wrapper-class compare() methods -- is the idiomatic, safe choice inside any compareTo() or Comparator, rather than hand-rolled subtraction.

assessments.prompt: A Product class already implements Comparable<Product> to sort by price ascending. A specific report needs Products sorted by name instead, just for that one report. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Change Product's compareTo() to compare by name instead of price, since a class should only ever need one ordering at a time.
Add a second compareTo() method to Product that takes no arguments and compares by name.
Write a separate Comparator<Product> that compares by name, and pass it to sort() only where the report needs that specific order, leaving Product's compareTo() untouched.
This isn't possible in Java -- once a class implements Comparable, no other ordering can ever be used to sort it.
assessments.explanation: A Comparator is exactly the tool for a one-off or context-specific ordering that shouldn't change the class's own natural order: writing Comparator.comparing(Product::getName) and passing it to sort() for that one report leaves Product's existing compareTo() (and every other piece of code relying on its price-based natural order) completely unaffected. Option A would break every other place in the codebase that currently relies on Product's natural price ordering, just to satisfy one report's different need. Option B describes something Java doesn't support -- compareTo() cannot be overloaded with a no-argument version; Comparable<T> mandates exactly one compareTo(T) signature. Option D is false -- sort() and List.sort() both readily accept an explicit Comparator that overrides the natural order for that specific call, which is precisely the mechanism this scenario calls for.

assessments.prompt: Explain the structural difference between Comparable and Comparator -- not just what each one is used for, but why a class can only have one Comparable ordering while supporting unlimited Comparators, and when you'd reach for each.
assessments.modelAnswer: Comparable<T> is a capability a class bakes into itself, once: implementing it means writing a single method, compareTo(T other), that defines the one ordering the class's own author considers 'natural' for that type -- and because it's exactly one method with exactly one required signature, a class can express exactly one Comparable ordering, never several. Comparator<T>, by contrast, is not a method on the class being ordered at all -- it's a completely separate object, implementing its own single method, compare(T a, T b), that some other piece of code writes to express whatever ordering it happens to need at that moment. Because a Comparator lives outside the class it orders, entirely, nothing stops any number of different Comparators from existing for the same type simultaneously, each expressing a different ordering, defined by different pieces of code, for different purposes, with zero coordination required between them and zero changes needed to the class itself. This asymmetry maps directly onto when to reach for each: Comparable is the right choice when a type genuinely has one obvious, intrinsic ordering that essentially everyone using that type would expect by default -- numbers ordering by magnitude, dates ordering chronologically -- and baking that into the class itself means callers get correct default sorting for free, with no per-call setup. Comparator is the right choice for every other ordering need: sorting by a different field, sorting in reverse, sorting by a combination of fields with specific tie-breaking rules, or sorting a type that has no obvious natural order at all (or one whose source code you don't even have access to modify). In real code, it's completely normal for a type to define one sensible Comparable natural order and still have several different Comparators defined elsewhere for specific contexts that need something else -- the two mechanisms are complementary, not competing.

assessments.prompt: Comparator<Student> cmp = Comparator.comparing((Student s) -> s.grade).thenComparing(s -> s.gpa, Comparator.reverseOrder()); Two students, X (grade "B", gpa 3.5) and Y (grade "A", gpa 2.0), are compared with cmp.compare(X, Y). What does this comparison actually decide on, and what is the result's sign?
options: It decides based on gpa first, since thenComparing was written second in the chain but is actually evaluated with higher priority than comparing.

It decides based on grade alone, since "B".compareTo("A") is already nonzero -- gpa is never even consulted for this particular pair, because thenComparing only breaks ties when the primary comparison returns exactly zero. The result is positive, since "B" sorts after "A".
It throws an exception, because the two students differ in both grade and gpa at the same time.
It returns zero, treating X and Y as equal, because the chain combines both criteria into a single averaged comparison.
assessments.explanation: thenComparing is a tie-breaker, consulted only when the comparison before it in the chain returns exactly zero. Comparing X and Y by grade alone already produces a nonzero result -- "B" comes after "A" alphabetically, so comparing((s) -> s.grade) returns a positive value for compare(X, Y) -- and that nonzero result is what the whole chain returns immediately, without ever reaching the gpa-based thenComparing at all. Option A reverses how the chain actually evaluates; earlier keys are checked first and take priority. Option C invents a failure mode chained Comparators simply don't have. Option D is wrong because Comparator chaining never averages or blends criteria -- each key is checked in strict sequence, only falling through to the next on an exact tie.

assessments.prompt: class Item implements Comparable<Item> { String label; int priority; public int compareTo(Item other) { return Integer.compare(priority, other.priority); } } -- equals() and hashCode() are left as Object's defaults. Item a = new Item("apple", 1); Item b = new Item("banana", 1); TreeSet<Item> set = new TreeSet<>(); set.add(a); set.add(b); System.out.println(set.size()); What prints, and why?
options: 2, because a and b are clearly different objects with different labels, so both are kept regardless of what compareTo() returns.

1, because TreeSet uses compareTo() as its sole notion of equality internally, and a.compareTo(b) returns 0 (same priority) -- so even though a and b are not .equals() to each other, TreeSet treats them as duplicates and keeps only one.
This throws an exception, because compareTo() returning 0 for two objects that are not .equals() violates a rule the compiler enforces.
2, because leaving equals() and hashCode() as Object's defaults makes TreeSet fall back to comparing object identity instead of using compareTo() at all.
assessments.explanation: Unlike HashSet, which uses equals()/hashCode() to detect duplicates, TreeSet (and TreeMap) use compareTo() -- or a supplied Comparator -- as their entire notion of 'are these the same element' internally. a and b both have priority 1, so a.compareTo(b) is 0, and TreeSet treats that as 'already present,' silently keeping only the first one added and discarding the second, regardless of the fact that their labels differ and they are not .equals(). Option A assumes TreeSet checks equals(), which it specifically does not for this purpose. Option C invents a compiler-enforced consistency rule between compareTo() and equals() that doesn't actually exist -- it's a strongly recommended convention, not something Java checks or rejects. Option D is wrong because TreeSet's behavior here is not conditional on what equals()/hashCode() happen to be; it always uses compareTo()/Comparator for its internal ordering and duplicate detection.
